questions.knowledge_point: Applying Properties of Tautologies and Contradictions
questions.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\text{t}$ is a tautology, and $\text{c}$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∨\text{t}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{c}∧\text{c}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $¬P∧\text{t}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{c}∨P$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∨\text{t}$ | $\text{t}$ |
| $\text{c}∧\text{c}$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $¬P∧\text{t}$ | $¬P$ |
| $\text{c}∨P$ | $P$ |

questions.problem: Simplify the expression $[(P⇒¬Q)∧P]∧Q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

- First, we use the associative law:

$$
[(P⇒¬Q)∧P]∧Q≡(P⇒¬Q)∧(P∧Q)
$$

- Then, we use that $X⇒Y≡¬X∨Y:$

$$
(P⇒¬Q)∧(P∧Q)≡(¬P∨¬Q)∧(P∧Q)
$$

- Next, we use a De Morgan's law:

$$
(¬P∨¬Q)∧(P∧Q)≡¬(P∧Q)∧(P∧Q)
$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and its negation is a contradiction:

$$
¬(P∧Q)∧(P∧Q)≡c
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
[(P⇒¬Q)∧P]∧Q≡c.
$$

questions.problem: Simplify the expression $A∧(A⇒B).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

- First, we use that $X⇒Y≡¬X∨Y:$

$$
A∧(A⇒B)≡A∧(¬A∨B)
$$

- Then, we use the distributive law (disjunction over conjunction):

$$
A∧(¬A∨B)≡(A∧¬A)∨(A∧B)
$$

- Next,  we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and its negation is a contradiction:

$$
(A∧¬A)∨(A∧B)≡c∨(A∧B)
$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the disjunction of a statement and a contradiction equals the original statement:

$$
c∨(A∧B)≡(A∧B)
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
A∧(A⇒B)≡A∧B
$$

- Next,  we use a De Morgan's law:

$$
(X∧Y)∨(¬X∨¬Y)≡(X∧Y)∨¬(X∧Y)

- Finally, we use the fact that the disjunction of a statement and its negation is a tautology:

$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
[(X∧Y)∨¬X]∨¬Y≡t.
$$

questions.problem: Simplify the expression $¬[¬A∨(A∧¬B)].$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

- First, we use a De Morgan's law:

$$
¬[¬A∨(A∧¬B)]≡¬¬A∧¬(A∧¬B)
$$

- Next, we simplify the double negation:

$$
¬¬A∧¬(A∧¬B)≡A∧¬(A∧¬B)
$$

- Then, we use a De Morgan's law:

$$
A∧¬(A∧¬B)≡A∧(¬A∨¬¬B)
$$

- Next, we simplify the double negation:

$$
A∧(¬A∨¬¬B)≡A∧(¬A∨B)
$$

- Then, we use the distributive law (conjunction over disjunction):

$$
A∧(¬A∨B)≡(A∧¬A)∨(A∧B)
$$

- Next, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and its negation is a contradiction:

$$
(A∧¬A)∨(A∧B)≡c∨(A∧B)
$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the disjunction of a statement and a contradiction equals the original statement:

$$
c∨(A∧B)≡A∧B
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
¬[¬A∨(A∧¬B)]≡A∧B.
$$

Complete the truth table below and use it to determine whether $(A \land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A)$ is a tautology.

| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |

| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An expression is a tautology if it is always true, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, B \Rightarrow A \,$ | $\, (A\land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

According to the table, $(A \land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A)$ is always true. Therefore, it is a tautology.

canonical_examples.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\textbf t$ is a tautology, and $\textbf c$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\textbf t \land \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
| $\textbf t \lor \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
| $P \land \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
| $P \lor \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\textbf t \land \textbf  c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textbf c}$ |
| $\textbf t \lor \textbf  c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textbf t}$ |
| $P \land \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textbf c}$ |
| $P \lor \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}P}$ |
